params.title: Principles
params.subtitle: Electrical units, magnetism, materials, components, AC measurements, waveforms and conduction: the basics the exam builds on.

onScreen: Principles
Units, magnetism, materials, components, AC values, waveforms and conduction
scenes.narration: This lesson covers the electrical principles the Element 3 exam builds on. We'll name the basic units of power and energy, see how magnetism works, and compare materials. Then we'll look at resistors, capacitors, inductors and semiconductors, and learn the AC, or alternating current, values you'll measure: root mean square, or RMS, peak and peak-to-peak. We'll finish with waveforms and conduction. Let's start with the electrical elements: power, energy and reactance.

params.title: Apparent, true and reactive power
rows: AC voltmeter reading × AC ammeter reading
Out of phase; stored and returned, no net work

onScreen: Apparent power: voltmeter × ammeter, in volt-amperes
True power: watts, needs the power factor
Watt: 1 joule per second, or 1 volt × 1 ampere
Reactive power: VAR, stored and returned, no net work
scenes.narration: Multiply the reading of an AC voltmeter by the reading of an AC ammeter, and you get apparent power, measured in volt-amperes. That isn't true power, because the voltage and current may be out of phase. True power also needs the power factor, and it's measured in watts. The watt is the basic unit of electrical power: 1 joule per second, or 1 volt times 1 ampere. Reactive power is the out-of-phase power associated with inductors and capacitors. It's measured in VAR, volt-amperes reactive. It is stored and returned each cycle, so it does no net work.

params.title: Where energy is stored
items: A capacitor stores energy in the electrostatic field between its plates
An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field instead
Energy stored in an electrostatic field is measured in joules
Coulombs measure charge; watts measure the rate of energy flow

onScreen: Capacitor: electrostatic field between the plates
Inductor: magnetic field
Stored energy: joules
Coulombs: charge; watts: rate of energy flow
scenes.narration: Where does a capacitor keep its energy? In the electrostatic field between its plates. An inductor is different: it stores energy in a magnetic field instead. The amount of electrical energy stored in an electrostatic field is expressed in joules, the unit of energy. Don't mix that up with coulombs, which measure electric charge, or with watts, which measure the rate at which energy flows.

params.title: Inductive reactance of a coil
steps: 1 / 2π f C is capacitive reactance, not inductive
params.answer: Coil reactance: X<sub>L</sub> = 2π f L, in ohms

onScreen: X sub L = 2π f L
f in hertz, L in henrys
X sub L in ohms
1 / 2π f C is capacitive reactance
scenes.narration: To find the inductive reactance of a coil from its frequency and inductance, use X sub L equals two pi f L. Here f is the frequency in hertz, L is the inductance in henrys, and the answer, X sub L, comes out in ohms. Watch for the look-alike, 1 over two pi f C. That form is capacitive reactance, for a capacitor, not inductive reactance. So for a coil, X sub L equals two pi f L, in ohms.

blocks.label: Current through a conductor
blocks.note: Double the current, double the field

blocks.label: Magnetic field
blocks.note: Strength set by the amount of current

blocks.label: Voltage with no current
blocks.note: Unconnected DC source or charged capacitor

onScreen: Current through a conductor makes a magnetic field
Field strength set by the amount of current
Voltage with no current: no magnetic field
scenes.narration: A current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it. The strength of that field is determined by the amount of current: double the current, and the field doubles. Voltage alone isn't enough. An unconnected DC, or direct current, source has voltage across its terminals, and so does a charged capacitor. But with no current flowing, neither of them produces a magnetic field. Remember it this way: current makes magnetism.

params.title: Lenz's law and back EMF
items: Lenz's law: induced currents produce expanding fields that oppose the original field
Back EMF: a voltage that opposes the applied EMF
It is induced by a coil's own changing magnetic field
Back EMF is a voltage, not a current
Both oppose the change that caused them

onScreen: Lenz's law: induced fields oppose the original field
Back EMF opposes the applied EMF
Induced by the coil's own changing field
A voltage, not a current
scenes.narration: These ideas share a theme: opposition. When induced currents produce expanding magnetic fields that oppose the original magnetic field, that's Lenz's law. A coil shows the same kind of opposition. Back EMF, or back electromotive force, is a voltage that opposes the applied EMF. It is induced by the coil's own changing magnetic field. Notice that back EMF is a voltage, not a current. Lenz's law and back EMF both oppose the change that caused them.

params.title: Reluctance and permeability
rows: Opposition to creating magnetic lines of force

onScreen: Reluctance: opposition to creating magnetic lines of force
The magnetic counterpart of resistance
Permeability: flux density ÷ magnetizing force
Iron and ferrite: high permeability
scenes.narration: Next, a pair of magnetic terms. In a magnetic circuit, reluctance is the opposition to the creation of magnetic lines of force. Think of it as the magnetic counterpart of resistance. Permeability is the ratio of the magnetic flux density in a substance to the magnetizing force that produces it. Iron and ferrite have high permeability.

params.title: Corrosion in seawater
items: Galvanic corrosion: current flow between dissimilar metals
Stray current corrosion: driven by an outside source instead
Zinc bar: sacrificial anode, more active than bronze, steel and copper
Stainless steel propeller shaft: may be least affected
Aluminum outdrive: corrodes readily

onScreen: Galvanic corrosion: current between dissimilar metals
Stray current corrosion: outside source
Zinc bar: sacrificial anode
Stainless steel propeller shaft: least affected
Aluminum outdrive: corrodes readily
scenes.narration: Now materials, starting with corrosion. Corrosion resulting from electric current flow between dissimilar metals is called galvanic corrosion. Stray current corrosion is different: it's driven by an outside source instead. To protect a vessel, a zinc bar is usually employed as a sacrificial anode. Zinc is more active than the vessel's bronze, steel and copper fittings, so the zinc corrodes instead of them. Of common underwater fittings in seawater, a stainless steel propeller shaft may be least affected by galvanic corrosion, while an aluminum outdrive corrodes readily.

blocks.label: Lower frequency
blocks.note: Current uses more of the conductor

blocks.label: Frequency increases
blocks.note: RF current flows in a thin surface layer

blocks.label: AC resistance rises
blocks.note: Less of the conductor carries current

onScreen: Lower frequency: current uses more of the conductor
Higher frequency: RF current in a thin surface layer
AC resistance rises
scenes.narration: Next, the skin effect. At lower frequencies, current uses more of the conductor. But as the frequency increases, RF, or radio frequency, current flows in a thinner and thinner layer of the conductor, closer to its surface. That phenomenon is called skin effect. With less of the conductor carrying the current, its AC resistance goes up.

params.title: Dielectrics and UHF insulators
rows: Relative dielectric constant 1, as in a vacuum
Best UHF insulator: very low dielectric loss

onScreen: Air: relative dielectric constant 1, same as a vacuum
Mica: best UHF insulator, very low loss
Rubber and wax impregnated paper: lossy
Lead: a conductor, not an insulator
scenes.narration: Insulators matter too. The relative dielectric constant for air is 1, the same value defined for a vacuum. At UHF, ultra high frequency, mica is the most useful insulator, because its dielectric loss is very low. Rubber and wax impregnated paper become lossy at those frequencies. And lead doesn't belong on the list at all: it's a conductor, not an insulator.

params.title: Combining inductors and capacitors
steps: Series inductors add like series resistors
Sum of reciprocals: capacitors in series
params.answer: Series inductors and parallel capacitors add

onScreen: Series inductors: L sub T = L sub 1 + L sub 2
Reciprocal formula is for parallel inductors
Parallel capacitors: C sub T = C sub 1 + C sub 2 + C sub 3
Sum of reciprocals is for series capacitors
scenes.narration: Now resistance, capacitance and inductance. The total inductance of inductors in series is L sub T equals L sub 1 plus L sub 2. Series inductors add just like series resistors. The reciprocal formula is for inductors in parallel. Capacitors work the other way around. The total capacitance of 3 capacitors in parallel is C sub T equals C sub 1 plus C sub 2 plus C sub 3. The sum-of-reciprocals formula is for capacitors in series. So series inductors and parallel capacitors simply add.

blocks.label: Supply line
blocks.note: DC with unwanted AC riding on it

blocks.label: Bypass capacitor
blocks.note: Low impedance path for AC; blocks DC

onScreen: Supply line: DC with unwanted AC
DC continues to the circuit
Bypass capacitor: low impedance path for AC, blocks DC
AC removed to ground
scenes.narration: Here a supply line carries DC, with some unwanted AC riding on it, and the circuit needs only the DC. A bypass capacitor removes the alternating current by providing a low impedance path to ground. The AC takes that easy path and is gone. The capacitor blocks DC, so the DC continues along the line to the circuit.

params.title: What makes a good conductor
items: Many free electrons, loosely bound to their atoms
Best low-resistance conductors: gold, silver and copper
Higher resistance: stainless steel, bronze, lead, iron, nickel, zinc, manganese

onScreen: Many loosely bound free electrons
Best: gold, silver and copper
Higher resistance: stainless steel, bronze, lead, iron, nickel, zinc, manganese
scenes.narration: Why do some metals conduct better than others? Good conductors, with minimum resistance, have many free electrons, loosely bound to their atoms and free to move. Gold, silver and copper are the best low-resistance conductors. Stainless steel, bronze, lead, iron, nickel, zinc and manganese all have higher resistance.

onScreen: Fewer turns: less inductance
More turns: more inductance
More core permeability: more inductance
Compressed turns: more inductance
scenes.narration: To reduce the inductance of an antenna coil, reduce the number of turns. That's the only change here that lowers it. Adding turns raises the inductance. So does adding core permeability, for example with an iron or ferrite core. And so does compressing the turns closer together. If the question asks how to reduce inductance, the answer is fewer turns.

params.title: Junction diode ratings
items: Most used specs: maximum forward current and PIV, peak inverse voltage
Junction temperature limits the maximum forward current
Exceed the junction temperature limit and the diode is destroyed

onScreen: Specs: maximum forward current and PIV
Junction temperature limits forward current
Exceeding it destroys the diode
scenes.narration: On to semiconductors. The 2 most commonly used specifications for a junction diode are its maximum forward current and its PIV, peak inverse voltage. What limits the maximum forward current? The junction temperature. Push too much current through the diode and the junction gets too hot. Exceed that limit and the diode is destroyed.

onScreen: JFET, MOSFET and GaAsFET: separate FET families
JFET types: N-channel and P-channel
MOSFET: Zener diode in the gate protects the gate oxide
scenes.narration: FETs, or field-effect transistors, come in separate families: the JFET, or junction field-effect transistor, the MOSFET, or metal oxide semiconductor field-effect transistor, and the GaAsFET, a gallium arsenide FET. The 2 basic types of junction field-effect transistor are N-channel and P-channel. MOSFETs and GaAsFETs are separate FET families, not JFET types. MOSFETs are built with a Zener diode in their gate. It protects the thin gate oxide from static charges and excessive voltages.

params.title: FET versus bipolar, emitter versus collector
rows: Low input impedance: the base draws current

onScreen: FET: high input impedance
Bipolar: low input impedance, base draws current
Common emitter: more voltage gain
Common collector: gain slightly below 1
scenes.narration: A pair of comparisons the exam likes. Start with input impedance. An FET has high input impedance. A bipolar transistor has low input impedance, because its base draws current. Now voltage gain. A common emitter amplifier has more voltage gain than a common collector amplifier. The common collector's voltage gain is slightly below 1.

callouts.label: Shows the effective, or RMS, value of the AC current
RMS = root mean square; there is no such measure as TRM

onScreen: AC ammeter: effective, or RMS, values
RMS: root mean square, not TRM
Household outlet: 117 V AC RMS
scenes.narration: Now electrical measurements. An AC ammeter indicates effective values of current, called RMS values. RMS stands for root mean square. Watch out for T R M: there's no such measure. An AC voltmeter reads RMS values too, and the RMS voltage at a common household electrical power outlet is 117 volts AC.

params.title: Household AC: RMS, peak and peak-to-peak
labels: Peak-to-peak: 331 V, from top to bottom

onScreen: RMS: 117 volts
Peak-to-peak: 331 volts
scenes.narration: Here's a sine wave we'll keep coming back to: the household outlet. Its RMS voltage is 117 volts. The peak voltage, at the top of the wave, is higher: 117 times the square root of 2, or 165.5 volts. Measured from the positive peak all the way down to the negative peak, the peak-to-peak voltage is 331 volts. Don't confuse them: 165.5 volts is the peak, and 331 volts is peak-to-peak.

params.title: From meter reading to peak and average

onScreen: Peak = RMS reading × 1.414
Peak × 0.707 = RMS
Average = RMS reading × 0.9
scenes.narration: To get the peak voltage from an AC voltmeter reading, multiply the reading by 1.414. For the household outlet, 117 volts times the square root of 2, which is about 1.414, gives 165.5 volts peak. Multiplying by 0.707 does the opposite: it takes you from peak back to RMS. And to obtain the average voltage, multiply the voltmeter reading by 0.9. So remember: 1.414 for peak, 0.9 for average.

params.title: Reading a sine wave on an oscilloscope

callouts.label: A pure sine wave on the graticule, the grid on the screen
Peak-to-peak: easiest to measure, read straight off the graticule

onScreen: Pure sine wave on the graticule
Peak-to-peak: easiest amplitude to measure
scenes.narration: Now put a pure sine wave on an oscilloscope. Which voltage amplitude is easiest to measure? Peak-to-peak. You read it straight off the graticule, the measuring grid on the screen, from the top of the wave to the bottom. No other amplitude is as easy to read directly on the screen.

params.title: Where the sine wave comes from
labels: Amplitude: projection of a point on a wheel turning at uniform speed

onScreen: Point on a wheel rotating at uniform speed
1 complete cycle: 360 degrees
Each half cycle: 180 degrees
scenes.narration: On to waveforms. Where does the sine wave's shape come from? Picture a point on a wheel rotating at a uniform speed. A sine wave's amplitude at any given instant can be represented by the projection of that point. A full turn of the wheel traces 1 complete cycle, and there are 360 degrees in 1 complete sine wave cycle. Each half cycle spans 180 degrees.

params.title: The square wave
labels: Stays at each level for equal amounts of time
Made of the fundamental plus all the odd harmonics

onScreen: Abrupt changes between 2 voltage levels
Equal time at each level
Fundamental plus all odd harmonics
scenes.narration: A square wave abruptly changes back and forth between 2 voltage levels, and it stays at these levels for equal amounts of time. What is it made of? Sine waves: the fundamental frequency and all the odd harmonics. Add odd harmonics to the fundamental, and the edges sharpen toward a square.

params.title: Square wave versus sawtooth wave
rows: Fundamental + all harmonics, even and odd
A slow ramp and a fast edge
Rise much faster than fall, or vice versa

onScreen: Square wave: fundamental plus odd harmonics
Sawtooth wave: fundamental plus all harmonics, even and odd
Square: rises and falls equally fast
Sawtooth: rise much faster than fall, or vice versa
scenes.narration: Now compare the square wave with the sawtooth wave. A sawtooth wave is made up of sine waves at the fundamental frequency and all the harmonics, even and odd. The square wave uses only the odd ones. A square wave sits at 2 levels for equal times. A sawtooth wave is characterized by a rise time significantly faster than its fall time, or the other way around. A square wave rises and falls equally fast.

params.title: RMS: the effective value
labels: Same heating in a resistor as 117 V DC

onScreen: RMS: 117 volts AC
Same heating in a resistor as 117 volts DC
Peak 165.5 volts, peak-to-peak 331 volts
scenes.narration: Now conduction, and back to our sine wave. Why is RMS called the effective value? Root mean square is the AC voltage that causes the same heating in a resistor as a corresponding value of DC voltage. So 117 volts RMS heats a resistor just as much as 117 volts DC, even though the wave's peak reaches 165.5 volts and its peak-to-peak is 331 volts. That equal heating is why RMS is also called the effective value.

params.title: True power
params.formula: True power = apparent power × power factor
steps: RMS voltage × RMS current = apparent power only
True power is the power actually dissipated
Reactive power swaps between fields, not dissipated
params.answer: Out of phase: apparent power × power factor

onScreen: True power = apparent power × power factor
RMS voltage × RMS current: apparent power only
True power: the power dissipated
Reactive power alternates between fields, not dissipated
scenes.narration: When AC voltage and current are out of phase, how much power is really dissipated? To find the true power, multiply the apparent power by the power factor. Multiplying RMS voltage by RMS current alone gives only the apparent power. True power is the power actually dissipated. Where does the rest go? In a circuit with both inductors and capacitors, the reactive power alternates between the magnetic and electric fields. It is not dissipated.

params.title: Conductivity and cross-sectional area
items: Descending conductivity: silver, copper, aluminum, iron, lead
Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area
Halve the cross-sectional area and the resistance doubles

onScreen: Descending conductivity: silver, copper, aluminum, iron, lead
Resistance inversely proportional to area
Half the area: double the resistance
scenes.narration: Common materials in order of descending conductivity are silver, copper, aluminum, iron and lead. Silver conducts best, and lead is the poorest of these. The size of the conductor matters too. Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. So halving the cross-sectional area of a conductor doubles its resistance.

onScreen: Source with fixed internal resistance
Load impedance equals the source's internal impedance
Maximum power transferred
scenes.narration: Last, getting the most power out of a source. Every source has some internal resistance. With that internal resistance fixed, maximum power is transferred to the load when the load impedance equals the internal impedance of the source. Match the load to the source, and the load gets the most power.
